🚨 One College Per Week 👉 GONE

We’re now seeing warnings that colleges—particularly small private colleges—could begin closing or merging at an extraordinary pace.

Moody’s has turned negative on the higher-education sector, and research highlighted by Fortune suggests that more than one-quarter of America’s roughly 1,700 private nonprofit four-year colleges could be at risk of closing, merging or reaching serious financial distress over the next decade.

And colleges have already been closing or merging at roughly one per week by some recent measures.

The conventional explanation you’re going to hear is the “demographic cliff”: birth rates declined after the 2008 financial crisis, so there are fewer college-age kids coming into the system.

I think the demographic cliff is exposing a business model—and perhaps an institution—that was already losing the support of the American public.

For decades, colleges operated under the assumption that tuition could keep rising, students would continue borrowing enormous amounts of money, enrollment would continue growing, and families would continue believing that virtually any four-year degree justified the cost.

That assumption is breaking down.

Families are questioning whether a $50,000-, $60,000- or $80,000-a-year education produces enough economic value to justify the price.

Students now have alternatives: community college, trade schools, apprenticeships, certifications, online education and entering the workforce directly.

Meanwhile, many colleges carry enormous fixed costs—administration, buildings, dormitories, athletics, debt and infrastructure. Private colleges increasingly have to discount their advertised tuition heavily just to convince students to attend.

But there is another piece of this that can’t be ignored:

AMERICANS ARE LOSING CONFIDENCE IN HIGHER EDUCATION

2015: 57% of Americans had a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education.

2018: 48%
2023: 36%
2024: 36%
2025: 42%
2026: 38%

So despite a brief rebound in 2025, confidence in higher education has fallen 19 percentage points in just 11 years.

Among the primary reasons Americans themselves give for lacking confidence in higher education are:

• Cost
• Perceived political agendas
• The nature of instruction

That introduces something beyond demographics and economics:

A cultural problem.

For generations, sending your child to college was almost automatically viewed as a positive thing—an investment in their future.

Today, some families are asking a completely different set of questions.

Is this degree worth the money?

Will it actually improve my child’s career prospects?

Is taking on this debt worthwhile?

And increasingly:

Do I agree with what this institution is teaching my child?

Put everything together:

HIGH TUITION

STUDENT DEBT

QUESTIONABLE ROI FOR SOME DEGREES

MASSIVE FIXED COSTS

AGGRESSIVE TUITION DISCOUNTING

MORE ALTERNATIVE CAREER PATHS

DECLINING PUBLIC CONFIDENCE

CONCERNS ABOUT POLITICAL AGENDAS AND INSTRUCTION

You’re left with a higher-education model that had already become too large, too expensive, too dependent upon debt and continuously increasing enrollment—and, for a significant portion of Americans, increasingly disconnected from what they want from higher education.

That creates a vicious cycle:

Fewer students → greater tuition discounts → lower net tuition revenue → cuts to programs and staff → weaker institutions → fewer students.

Eventually, the math stops working.

If more than one-quarter of America’s private nonprofit colleges really are approaching serious financial stress at the same time that public confidence in higher education has fallen from 57% to 38%, we may be witnessing the beginning of one of the largest consolidations of American higher education in generations.

⚖️ JAG: THE MILITARY–CIVILIAN JUSTICE CLUSTER JUST EXPANDED AGAIN

We’ve been tracking an unusual series of developments involving the boundary between the military justice system and civilian federal courts.

Now there’s another significant addition.

🇺🇸 SEPTEMBER 24 — JAG PROSECUTOR MODEL EXPANDS TO THREE MORE FEDERAL DISTRICTS

According to a Defense Department email reviewed by Bloomberg Law, DOJ is seeking active-duty and reserve military attorneys to serve as temporary Special Assistant U.S. Attorneys in:

📍 Manhattan — Southern District of New York
📍 Los Angeles — Central District of California
📍 Sacramento — Eastern District of California

The assignments are expected to last 179 days (that’s a 17 🐸), beginning October 13 or later, and are expected to focus primarily on immigration-related prosecutions.

But this is important:

THESE ARE NOT THE FIRST CITIES.

We’ve already documented JAG/military attorneys being inserted into civilian federal prosecution roles in several other jurisdictions.

🇺🇸 WASHINGTON, D.C.
In August 2025, U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro requested 20 military lawyers to help handle the increased prosecutorial caseload created by the federal law-enforcement surge. The Pentagon approved the request. 

🇺🇸 MEMPHIS, TENNESSEE
In January 2026, DOJ formally announced that 20 military JAG attorneys from all four branches had been assigned as Special Assistant U.S. Attorneys to prosecute federal cases associated with the Memphis Safe Task Force. DOJ itself described the DOJ–military personnel-sharing arrangement as “unprecedented.” 

🇺🇸 MINNEAPOLIS / MINNESOTA
Military JAG attorneys were also assigned to assist federal prosecutors during the immigration-enforcement surge there. That deployment produced the May 1 court challenge we’ve been following, in which a Minnesota judge ruled that an active-duty Army JAG could legally prosecute a civilian as a Special Assistant U.S. Attorney. 

🇺🇸 LAS CRUCES, NEW MEXICO
DOJ announced in January that three military attorneys and two military paralegals had been assigned to the Las Cruces U.S. Attorney’s Office. The JAG SAUSAs are prosecuting federal border-related offenses including immigration, narcotics, firearms and human-smuggling cases. 

And the Pentagon had also ordered military lawyers for West Texas, including the El Paso/Del Rio region, as part of the broader expansion of military legal personnel supporting DOJ operations. 

So now look at the footprint:

WASHINGTON, D.C.

SACRAMENTO

And remember the legal framework that developed alongside it.

⚖️ MAY 1, 2026
A federal judge ruled military attorneys may prosecute civilians as SAUSAs when properly detailed to DOJ.

⚖️ SEPTEMBER 1, 2026
The D.C. Circuit ruled that an ordinary civilian district court could not simply vacate a military court-martial judgment.

⚖️ SEPTEMBER 24, 2026
The government is now preparing to expand the JAG-as-federal-prosecutor model into three additional major federal districts.

There’s also an important legal limitation here: DOJ’s Office of Legal Counsel concluded that the Posse Comitatus Act does not bar these arrangements when the military attorneys are detailed full-time and operate under civilian DOJ control and supervision. 

Something unusual is clearly happening:

MILITARY LAWYERS ARE BECOMING AN INCREASINGLY NORMAL PART OF THE CIVILIAN FEDERAL PROSECUTION SYSTEM.

What began as a limited deployment is now spreading across multiple federal districts.

That is exactly why we’ve been tracking this as a distinct cluster:

⚖️ MILITARY JUSTICE ↔ CIVILIAN JUSTICE

The boundary keeps getting tested, defined—and expanded.
